name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q01 - Historical contributions to periodic classification

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists listed in Column I with their corresponding contributions to the development of the periodic table in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Johann Dobereiner (i) Plotted physical properties like atomic volume against atomic weight
(B) John Alexander Newlands (ii) Observed regularities in X-ray spectra plotting \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against \(Z\)
(C) Lothar Meyer (iii) Formulated the Law of Triads based on atomic weight relationships
(D) Henry Moseley (iv) Proposed the Law of Octaves comparing elements to musical notes

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical contribution of Johann Dobereiner
In early 1800s, Johann Dobereiner observed that in certain groups of three elements (Triads), the middle element had an atomic weight approximately midway between the atomic weights of the other two members, and its chemical properties were intermediate.

Step 2: Historical contribution of John Alexander Newlands
In 1865, John Alexander Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of their atomic weights and found that every eighth element exhibited properties similar to the first element, resembling octaves in music (Law of Octaves).

Step 3: Historical contribution of Lothar Meyer
In 1869, Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties such as atomic volume, melting point, and boiling point against atomic weight, obtaining a periodically repeating curve with changing length of repeating patterns.

Step 4: Contribution of Henry Moseley
In 1913, Henry Moseley examined characteristic X-ray spectra across elements and established that a plot of \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against atomic number (\(Z\)) gives a straight line, proving that atomic number is the fundamental property governing periodicity.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Johann Dobereiner matches with Formulated the Law of Triads based on atomic weight relationships; John Alexander Newlands matches with Proposed the Law of Octaves comparing elements to musical notes; Lothar Meyer matches with Plotted physical properties like atomic volume against atomic weight; Henry Moseley matches with Observed regularities in X-ray spectra plotting \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against \(Z\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q02 - Official names for superheavy elements

questiontext.text:
Match the atomic numbers of elements listed in Column I with their corresponding IUPAC official names given in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) 104 (i) Copernicium
(B) 106 (ii) Rutherfordium
(C) 112 (iii) Oganesson
(D) 118 (iv) Seaborgium

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Element with atomic number 104
The element with atomic number 104 has the systematic IUPAC name Unnilquadium (symbol Unq) and its officially ratified IUPAC name is Rutherfordium (Rf).

Step 2: Element with atomic number 106
The element with atomic number 106 has the systematic IUPAC name Unnilhexium (symbol Unh) and was officially named Seaborgium (Sg) in honour of Glenn T. Seaborg.

Step 3: Element with atomic number 112
The element with atomic number 112 has the systematic IUPAC name Ununbium (symbol Uub) and its officially assigned IUPAC name is Copernicium (Cn).

Step 4: Element with atomic number 118
The element with atomic number 118 is a noble gas element with systematic IUPAC name Ununoctium (symbol Uuo) and official IUPAC name Oganesson (Og).

Therefore, the correct matching is: 104 matches with Rutherfordium; 106 matches with Seaborgium; 112 matches with Copernicium; 118 matches with Oganesson.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q03 - Mendeleev predictions and periodic patterns

questiontext.text:
Match the items related to Mendeleev's periodic table in Column I with the corresponding descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Eka-Aluminium (i) Predicted element discovered later as Germanium with oxide \(\mathrm{EO_2}\)
(B) Eka-Silicon (ii) Lower atomic weight element placed after higher atomic weight element to maintain periodic family
(C) Tellurium and Iodine anomaly (iii) Oxide formula \(\mathrm{RO_3}\) representing the highest saline oxide
(D) Group VI elements in Mendeleev's table (iv) Predicted element discovered later as Gallium with oxide \(\mathrm{E_2O_3}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mendeleev's prediction for Eka-Aluminium
Mendeleev left a gap under aluminium and predicted an element termed Eka-Aluminium with an estimated atomic weight of 68 and oxide formula \(\mathrm{E_2O_3}\). This element was discovered later as Gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga_2O_3}\)).

Step 2: Mendeleev's prediction for Eka-Silicon
Mendeleev left a gap under silicon and predicted Eka-Silicon with an atomic weight of 72 and oxide formula \(\mathrm{EO_2}\). It was subsequently discovered as Germanium (\(\mathrm{GeO_2}\)).

Step 3: Tellurium and Iodine anomaly
Mendeleev placed iodine (atomic weight 126.9) in Group VII with the halogens after tellurium (atomic weight 127.6) in Group VI, disregarding strictly increasing atomic weights so that elements with similar properties remained in the same vertical column.

Step 4: Group VI higher oxide formula
In Mendeleev's published periodic system, elements belonging to Group VI have the characteristic highest saline oxide formula of \(\mathrm{RO_3}\) (such as \(\mathrm{SO_3}\), \(\mathrm{SeO_3}\), \(\mathrm{TeO_3}\)).

Therefore, the correct matching is: Eka-Aluminium matches with Predicted element discovered later as Gallium with oxide \(\mathrm{E_2O_3}\); Eka-Silicon matches with Predicted element discovered later as Germanium with oxide \(\mathrm{EO_2}\); Tellurium and Iodine anomaly matches with Lower atomic weight element placed after higher atomic weight element to maintain periodic family; Group VI elements in Mendeleev's table matches with Oxide formula \(\mathrm{RO_3}\) representing the highest saline oxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q04 - Periodic table blocks and electron configurations

questiontext.text:
Match the block/category of elements in Column I with their general outer electronic configurations in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) s-Block elements (i) \(\mathrm{(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}}\)
(B) p-Block elements (ii) \(\mathrm{ns^{1-2}}\)
(C) d-Block elements (iii) \(\mathrm{(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2}\)
(D) f-Block elements (iv) \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^{1-6}}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Outer electronic configuration of s-block elements
Elements of Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 2 (alkaline earth metals) have valence configurations of \(\mathrm{ns^1}\) and \(\mathrm{ns^2}\) respectively, yielding the general outer configuration \(\mathrm{ns^{1-2}}\).

Step 2: Outer electronic configuration of p-block elements
Elements of Groups 13 to 18 possess outer electronic configurations varying across periods from \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^1}\) to \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^6}\).

Step 3: Outer electronic configuration of d-block elements
Transition elements (Groups 3 to 12) involve the progressive filling of penultimate d-orbitals and possess the general outer configuration \(\mathrm{(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}}\) (for instance, Pd has \(\mathrm{4d^{10}5s^0}\)).

Step 4: Outer electronic configuration of f-block elements
Inner-transition elements comprising the lanthanoids and actinoids are characterized by the progressive filling of antipenultimate f-orbitals with the general outer configuration \(\mathrm{(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2}\).

Therefore, the correct matching is: s-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{ns^{1-2}}\); p-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{ns^2 np^{1-6}}\); d-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}}\); f-Block elements matches with \(\mathrm{(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q05 - Characteristic properties across periodic blocks

questiontext.text:
Match the groups/blocks of elements in Column I with their prominent chemical and physical features in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Group 1 (Alkali metals) (i) Possess large negative electron gain enthalpies and readily accept electrons
(B) Group 16 (Chalcogens) (ii) Exhibit variable oxidation states, coloured ions, and catalytic activity
(C) Groups 3 to 12 (Transition metals) (iii) Highly reactive metals with low ionization enthalpies forming \(1+\) ions
(D) Actinoids (iv) Radioactive series displaying a wide range of oxidation states due to small energy differences

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Properties of Group 1 elements
Alkali metals have low ionization enthalpies, lose their single valence electron readily to form \(1+\) cations, and are highly electropositive and reactive, forming predominantly ionic compounds.

Step 2: Properties of Group 16 elements
Chalcogens require two electrons to attain a stable octet noble gas configuration; they exhibit highly negative electron gain enthalpies and pronounced non-metallic character.

Step 3: Properties of Groups 3 to 12 elements
Transition metals are characterized by partially filled d-orbitals, variable oxidation states, coloured hydrated ions or complexes, paramagnetism, and frequent use as catalysts.

Step 4: Properties of Actinoids
Actinoids are radioactive elements where early members exhibit complicated chemistry with multiple oxidation states because 5f, 6d, and 7s energy levels are comparable in energy.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Group 1 (Alkali metals) matches with Highly reactive metals with low ionization enthalpies forming \(1+\) ions; Group 16 (Chalcogens) matches with Possess large negative electron gain enthalpies and readily accept electrons; Groups 3 to 12 (Transition metals) matches with Exhibit variable oxidation states, coloured ions, and catalytic activity; Actinoids matches with Radioactive series displaying a wide range of oxidation states due to small energy differences.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q06 - Anomalous behavior of second period elements

questiontext.text:
Match each anomalous property/behavior of second-period elements in Column I with its underlying scientific rationale in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Boron forms only \(\mathrm{[BF_4]^-}\) whereas aluminium forms \(\mathrm{[AlF_6]^{3-}}\) (i) Similarity in ionic potential (charge-to-radius ratio) and electronegativity
(B) Carbon and nitrogen readily form stable multiple bonds to themselves (ii) Small atomic size enabling effective sideways overlap of unhybridized \(2p\) orbitals
(C) Lithium and beryllium form compounds with pronounced covalent character (iii) Absence of \(d\)-orbitals restricting the maximum covalency to four
(D) Diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium (iv) Extremely small cation size resulting in exceptionally high polarising power

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Covalency limitation of boron
The second-period elements have only four valence orbitals (one \(2s\) and three \(2p\)) and lack \(d\)-orbitals. Therefore, the maximum covalency of boron is strictly four (as in \(\mathrm{[BF_4]^-}\)), while aluminium can expand its octet to six using vacant \(3d\) orbitals to form \(\mathrm{[AlF_6]^{3-}}\).

Step 2: Multiple bonding in second-period elements
Carbon and nitrogen have compact atomic radii, which allows their \(2p\) atomic orbitals to approach closely and form strong \(p_\pi - p_\pi\) multiple bonds with themselves and each other (e.g., \(\mathrm{C=C}\), \(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\), \(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\)).

Step 3: Covalent nature of lithium and beryllium compounds
Due to their very small ionic radii, \(\mathrm{Li^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Be^{2+}}\) have exceptionally high charge/radius ratios (polarising power), which polarises anions significantly and introduces substantial covalent character according to Fajan's rules.

Step 4: Diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium
Beryllium and aluminium resemble each other diagonally across the periodic table because the increase in size going down is compensated by the increase in charge and reduction in size going across, leading to similar charge-to-radius ratios and electronegativities.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Boron forms only \(\mathrm{[BF_4]^-}\) whereas aluminium forms \(\mathrm{[AlF_6]^{3-}}\) matches with Absence of \(d\)-orbitals restricting the maximum covalency to four; Carbon and nitrogen readily form stable multiple bonds to themselves matches with Small atomic size enabling effective sideways overlap of unhybridized \(2p\) orbitals; Lithium and beryllium form compounds with pronounced covalent character matches with Extremely small cation size resulting in exceptionally high polarising power; Diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium matches with Similarity in ionic potential (charge-to-radius ratio) and electronegativity.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q07 - Periodic trends in oxide acidity and basicity

questiontext.text:
Match the oxides listed in Column I with their correct chemical behavior in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) (i) Strongly acidic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) upon dissolution in water
(B) \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) (ii) Strongly basic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) upon reaction with water
(C) \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\) (iii) Neutral oxide that exhibits neither acidic nor basic properties
(D) \(\mathrm{CO}\) (iv) Amphoteric oxide that reacts with both strong acids and strong bases

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\)
Sodium is an electropositive alkali metal on the extreme left of the third period. Its normal oxide, \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\), reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{Na_2O + H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH}\)), demonstrating strong basicity.

Step 2: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)
Aluminium lies in the center of the third period. Its oxide, \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), is amphoteric; it dissolves in both acidic and basic solutions, forming aluminium salts and aluminate species respectively.

Step 3: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\)
Chlorine is an electronegative non-metal on the extreme right of the period. Its highest oxide, \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\), dissolves in water to form the strong acid perchloric acid (\(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HClO_4}\)), demonstrating strongly acidic nature.

Step 4: Chemical behavior of \(\mathrm{CO}\)
Carbon monoxide (\(\mathrm{CO}\)), along with \(\mathrm{NO}\) and \(\mathrm{N_2O}\), does not form salts with either acids or bases, classifying it as a neutral oxide.

Therefore, the correct matching is: \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) matches with Strongly basic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) upon reaction with water; \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) matches with Amphoteric oxide that reacts with both strong acids and strong bases; \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\) matches with Strongly acidic oxide that yields \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) upon dissolution in water; \(\mathrm{CO}\) matches with Neutral oxide that exhibits neither acidic nor basic properties.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q08 - Explanations for first ionization enthalpy anomalies

questiontext.text:
Match the comparative ionization enthalpy trends in Column I with the dominant governing factors responsible for them in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Boron has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Beryllium (i) Pairing of two electrons in the same \(2p\) orbital creates enhanced interelectronic repulsion
(B) Oxygen has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Nitrogen (ii) Single valence electron is located in a distant \(ns\) orbital well shielded by noble gas core
(C) Noble gases exhibit peak ionization enthalpies in each period (iii) Completely filled, closed valence shells possessing exceptionally high electronic stability
(D) Alkali metals display lowest first ionization enthalpies in each period (iv) Outermost electron resides in a \(2p\) orbital which is more shielded and less penetrating than a \(2s\) orbital

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: First ionization enthalpy difference between Boron and Beryllium
In beryllium (\(1s^2 2s^2\)), an electron is removed from a penetrating, fully filled \(2s\) subshell. In boron (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\)), the electron is removed from a \(2p\) subshell, which experiences greater shielding from the core \(1s\) and inner \(2s\) electrons and penetrates less toward the nucleus, making it easier to detach.

Step 2: First ionization enthalpy difference between Oxygen and Nitrogen
Nitrogen has an electronic configuration of \(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\), an extra-stable half-filled \(p\) subshell. Oxygen (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\)) contains two paired electrons in one of the \(2p\) orbitals. Mutual repulsion between these paired electrons facilitates the removal of the fourth \(2p\) electron.

Step 3: Exceptionally high ionization enthalpies of noble gases
Noble gases have completely filled valence shells (\(ns^2 np^6\), or \(1s^2\) for He). This closed electronic shell has maximum stability and large effective nuclear charge, requiring tremendous energy to remove an electron.

Step 4: Minimum ionization enthalpies of alkali metals
Alkali metals have a single valence \(ns^1\) electron situated outside a stable noble gas core. Because inner complete shells effectively screen the nuclear charge, this electron is held loosely and is detached with minimal energy.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Boron has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Beryllium matches with Outermost electron resides in a \(2p\) orbital which is more shielded and less penetrating than a \(2s\) orbital; Oxygen has a lower first ionization enthalpy than Nitrogen matches with Pairing of two electrons in the same \(2p\) orbital creates enhanced interelectronic repulsion; Noble gases exhibit peak ionization enthalpies in each period matches with Completely filled, closed valence shells possessing exceptionally high electronic stability; Alkali metals display lowest first ionization enthalpies in each period matches with Single valence electron is located in a distant \(ns\) orbital well shielded by noble gas core.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q09 - Periodic trends in electron gain enthalpy

questiontext.text:
Match the observations on electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{eg}H\)) in Column I with the corresponding scientific explanations in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Chlorine has a more negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than fluorine (i) Added electron must occupy an orbital in the next principal shell, yielding an unstable state
(B) Noble gases have positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) values (ii) Added electron enters a larger \(3p\) region of space with significantly lower electron repulsion
(C) Group 17 halogens have the highest negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (iii) Compact \(2p\) subshell results in strong repulsion that reduces enthalpy released compared to sulphur
(D) Oxygen has a less negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than sulphur (iv) High effective nuclear charge allows acquisition of a stable octet by adding a single electron

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reason for \(\Delta_{eg}H\) difference between chlorine and fluorine
In fluorine (\(n = 2\)), the incoming electron enters a very compact \(2p\) subshell and suffers substantial interelectronic repulsion. In chlorine (\(n = 3\)), the electron enters a more spacious \(3p\) orbital with much lower electron-electron repulsion, resulting in more heat released (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for Cl versus \(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for F).

Step 2: Reason for positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) of noble gases
Noble gas atoms have completely filled valence shells. An extra electron cannot be accommodated in the existing valence shell and must enter the next higher principal quantum shell, which requires energy input (endothermic process, positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\)).

Step 3: Reason for highly negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) of halogens
Halogens have a \(ns^2 np^5\) configuration with only one electron deficient from a stable octet and possess high effective nuclear charges across their periods, giving them a very strong tendency to gain an electron.

Step 4: Reason for \(\Delta_{eg}H\) difference between oxygen and sulphur
Similar to fluorine, oxygen has a very small atomic size (\(n = 2\)). The incoming electron added to oxygen experiences significant electron-electron repulsion, making its \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (\(-141\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) less negative than that of sulphur (\(-200\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Therefore, the correct matching is: Chlorine has a more negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than fluorine matches with Added electron enters a larger \(3p\) region of space with significantly lower electron repulsion; Noble gases have positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) values matches with Added electron must occupy an orbital in the next principal shell, yielding an unstable state; Group 17 halogens have the highest negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) matches with High effective nuclear charge allows acquisition of a stable octet by adding a single electron; Oxygen has a less negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) than sulphur matches with Compact \(2p\) subshell results in strong repulsion that reduces enthalpy released compared to sulphur.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q10 - Element reactivity from ionization enthalpy data

questiontext.text:
The first ionization enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H_1\)), second ionization enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H_2\)), and electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{eg}H\)) in \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) of four elements W, X, Y, and Z are provided below:

Element \(\Delta_i H_1\) \(\Delta_i H_2\) \(\Delta_{eg}H\)
W 2372 5251 +48
X 419 3051 -48
Y 1681 3374 -328
Z 520 7300 -60

Match the elements in Column I with their corresponding chemical descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
(A) Element W (i) Most reactive non-metal (Halogen)
(B) Element X (ii) Most reactive metal exhibiting the lowest \(\Delta_i H_1\)
(C) Element Y (iii) Least reactive element with noble gas electronic configuration
(D) Element Z (iv) Alkali metal forming predominantly covalent halides due to small size

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Element W
Element W exhibits an exceptionally high first ionization enthalpy (\(2372\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and a positive electron gain enthalpy (\(+48\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). This demonstrates a completely filled, closed electronic shell characteristic of noble gases (specifically Helium), making it the least reactive element.

Step 2: Evaluation of Element X
Element X has the lowest first ionization enthalpy among the metals listed (\(419\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) and a moderately large second ionization enthalpy (\(3051\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). This corresponds to Potassium, an alkali metal with the highest metallic reactivity.

Step 3: Evaluation of Element Y
Element Y possesses a very high first ionization enthalpy (\(1681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) together with a strongly negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). These values indicate a halogen atom (specifically Fluorine), which is the most reactive non-metal.

Step 4: Evaluation of Element Z
Element Z has a first ionization enthalpy of \(520\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) followed by an immense jump in its second ionization enthalpy to \(7300\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). This indicates a single valence electron outside a closed shell with very small ionic size (corresponding to Lithium). Due to the high polarising power of its cation, it forms halides with pronounced covalent character.

Therefore, the correct matching is: Element W matches with Least reactive element with noble gas electronic configuration; Element X matches with Most reactive metal exhibiting the lowest \(\Delta_i H_1\); Element Y matches with Most reactive non-metal (Halogen); Element Z matches with Alkali metal forming predominantly covalent halides due to small size.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q01 - Expected atomic weight of sodium in triad

questiontext.text: In Dobereiner's Law of Triads, the atomic weight of the central element is approximately equal to the arithmetic mean of the atomic weights of the first and third elements. If lithium has an atomic weight of \(7\) and potassium has an atomic weight of \(39\), calculate the expected atomic weight of sodium.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the given atomic weights
The atomic weight of lithium is \(7\) and the atomic weight of potassium is \(39\).

Step 2: Apply the arithmetic mean formula for Dobereiner's triad
The expected atomic weight of sodium is the average of lithium and potassium:
\[ \text{Atomic weight of Na} = \frac{7 + 39}{2} = \frac{46}{2} = 23 \]

Step 3: State the calculated numerical value
The resulting value is \(23\).

Final Answer: The expected atomic weight of sodium is 23.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q02 - Covalent radius of chlorine from bond distance

questiontext.text: The single bond internuclear distance between two chlorine atoms in a gaseous \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) molecule is \(198\text{ pm}\). Calculate the covalent radius of chlorine in picometres (\(\text{pm}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given internuclear distance
The bond length in the homonuclear diatomic \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) molecule is \(d(\mathrm{Cl-Cl}) = 198\text{ pm}\).

Step 2: Apply definition of covalent radius
For a homonuclear single-bonded diatomic molecule, the covalent radius is half of the internuclear bond distance:
\[ r_{\text{cov}}(\mathrm{Cl}) = \frac{d(\mathrm{Cl-Cl})}{2} = \frac{198\text{ pm}}{2} = 99\text{ pm} \]

Step 3: State the calculated numerical value
The covalent radius of chlorine is \(99\text{ pm}\).

Final Answer: The covalent radius of chlorine is 99 pm.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q03 - Metallic radius of copper from lattice spacing

questiontext.text: The distance between the nuclei of two adjacent copper atoms in solid metallic copper is \(256\text{ pm}\). Calculate the metallic radius of copper in picometres (\(\text{pm}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given internuclear distance
The distance separating adjacent copper metal cores in the metallic crystal is \(256\text{ pm}\).

Step 2: Apply definition of metallic radius
Metallic radius is defined as half the internuclear distance separating metal cores in the metallic lattice:
\[ r_{\text{met}}(\mathrm{Cu}) = \frac{256\text{ pm}}{2} = 128\text{ pm} \]

Step 3: State the calculated numerical value
The metallic radius of copper is \(128\text{ pm}\).

Final Answer: The metallic radius of copper is 128 pm.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q04 - Calculated atomic weight of strontium in triad

questiontext.text: In Dobereiner's alkaline earth metal triad, calcium has an atomic weight of \(40\) and barium has an atomic weight of \(137\). Calculate the expected arithmetic mean atomic weight of the middle element strontium.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given atomic weights
The atomic weight of calcium is \(40\) and the atomic weight of barium is \(137\).

Step 2: Compute arithmetic mean
According to Dobereiner's Law of Triads:
\[ \text{Mean atomic weight of Sr} = \frac{40 + 137}{2} = \frac{177}{2} = 88.5 \]

Step 3: State the calculated numerical value
The calculated mean atomic weight for strontium is \(88.5\).

Final Answer: The expected atomic weight of strontium is 88.5.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q05 - Calculated atomic weight of bromine in triad

questiontext.text: In Dobereiner's halogen triad, chlorine has an atomic weight of \(35.5\) and iodine has an atomic weight of \(127\). Calculate the expected arithmetic mean atomic weight of bromine.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given atomic weights
The atomic weight of chlorine is \(35.5\) and the atomic weight of iodine is \(127\).

Step 2: Calculate the mean value
According to Dobereiner's Law of Triads:
\[ \text{Mean atomic weight of Br} = \frac{35.5 + 127}{2} = \frac{162.5}{2} = 81.25 \]

Step 3: State the calculated numerical value
The expected arithmetic mean atomic weight of bromine is \(81.25\).

Final Answer: The expected atomic weight of bromine is 81.25.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q06 - Maximum number of elements in fifth period

questiontext.text: In the fifth period of the periodic table, the subshells filled in order of increasing energy are \(5s\), \(4d\), and \(5p\). Calculate the total number of elements that can be accommodated in this period.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Count available orbitals in the fifth period
The subshells filled in the fifth period are: one \(5s\) orbital, five \(4d\) orbitals, and three \(5p\) orbitals. Total number of orbitals is:
\[ 1 + 5 + 3 = 9\text{ orbitals} \]

Step 2: Determine maximum electron capacity
According to Pauli's exclusion principle, each orbital accommodates at most 2 electrons:
\[ 9\text{ orbitals} \times 2\text{ electrons/orbital} = 18\text{ electrons} \]

Step 3: Conclude the number of elements
Since each added electron corresponds to a distinct element, the fifth period contains exactly \(18\) elements.

Final Answer: The fifth period accommodates 18 elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q07 - Ionization enthalpy of atomic hydrogen from energy

questiontext.text: The energy of an electron in the ground state of a hydrogen atom is \(-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}\). Calculate the ionization enthalpy of atomic hydrogen in units of \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Take Avogadro's constant \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and round to the nearest integer).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate energy required to ionize a single hydrogen atom
Ionization enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from the ground state (\(n=1\)) to infinity (\(n=\infty\)):
\[ \Delta E = E_\infty - E_1 = 0 - (-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}) = +2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J per atom} \]

Step 2: Calculate energy per mole of hydrogen atoms
Multiplying by Avogadro's constant gives the energy per mole:
\[ \Delta_i H = (2.18 \times 10^{-18}\text{ J}) \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}) = 1.3128 \times 10^6\text{ J mol}^{-1} \]

Step 3: Convert to kilojoules per mole
Dividing by 1000:
\[ \Delta_i H = \frac{1.3128 \times 10^6\text{ J mol}^{-1}}{1000} \approx 1313\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \]

Final Answer: The ionization enthalpy of atomic hydrogen is 1313 kJ mol⁻¹.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_NUMERICAL_Q08 - Theoretical maximum elements in sixth period

questiontext.text: On the basis of quantum numbers, in the sixth period (\(n = 6\)), the subshells filled are \(6s\), \(4f\), \(5d\), and \(6p\). Calculate the theoretical maximum number of elements present in the sixth period of the periodic table.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Count the number of orbitals available in the sixth period
In the sixth period, the orbitals filled are: one \(6s\) orbital, seven \(4f\) orbitals, five \(5d\) orbitals, and three \(6p\) orbitals. Total number of available orbitals is:
\[ 1 + 7 + 5 + 3 = 16\text{ orbitals} \]

Step 2: Calculate the maximum electron capacity
Each orbital can accommodate at most 2 electrons with opposite spins:
\[ 16\text{ orbitals} \times 2\text{ electrons/orbital} = 32\text{ electrons} \]

Step 3: State the theoretical maximum number of elements
Therefore, the theoretical maximum number of elements in the sixth period is \(32\).

Final Answer: The theoretical maximum number of elements in the sixth period is 32.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q01 - Chronological sequence of periodic classification milestones

questiontext.text:
Consider the following historical milestones in the development of the periodic table:

  1. A.E.B. de Chancourtois arranges elements on a cylindrical table (telluric helix).
  2. Johann Dobereiner identifies Law of Triads in physical and chemical properties.
  3. Henry Moseley demonstrates that atomic number is the fundamental periodic property using X-ray spectra.
  4. John Alexander Newlands formulates the Law of Octaves.
  5. Dmitri Mendeleev publishes the Periodic Law based on atomic weights.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these historical events from earliest to latest?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Johann Dobereiner's Law of Triads
In the early 1800s (specifically 1829), German chemist Johann Dobereiner noted triads of elements where the middle element had an atomic weight approximately midway between the other two members.

Step 2: A.E.B. de Chancourtois's cylindrical helix
In 1862, French geologist A.E.B. de Chancourtois arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic weights on a cylinder to demonstrate periodic recurrence of properties.

Step 3: John Alexander Newlands's Law of Octaves
In 1865, English chemist John Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing atomic weights and noted that every eighth element exhibited properties similar to the first.

Step 4: Dmitri Mendeleev's Periodic Law
In 1869, Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev formulated and published the Periodic Law stating that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.

Step 5: Henry Moseley's Modern Periodic Law
In 1913, English physicist Henry Moseley discovered from characteristic X-ray spectra that atomic number (\(Z\)), rather than atomic mass, is the fundamental property governing elemental periodicity.

Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is: Dobereiner's Triads (1829) → de Chancourtois's cylindrical table (1862) → Newlands's Law of Octaves (1865) → Mendeleev's Periodic Law (1869) → Moseley's atomic number discovery (1913).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q02 - Increasing order of alkali metal atomic radii

questiontext.text:
Consider the alkali metals: \(\mathrm{Cs}\), \(\mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{Li}\), \(\mathrm{Na}\), and \(\mathrm{Rb}\).

Which of the following displays these elements arranged in the correct sequence of increasing atomic radius?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify group classification
Lithium (\(\mathrm{Li}\)), sodium (\(\mathrm{Na}\)), potassium (\(\mathrm{K}\)), rubidium (\(\mathrm{Rb}\)), and caesium (\(\mathrm{Cs}\)) all belong to Group 1 (alkali metals) with valence electronic configuration \(ns^1\).

Step 2: Trend of atomic radius down a group
Down a vertical column of the periodic table, the principal quantum number (\(n\)) increases with each successive element (from \(n=2\) for \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(n=6\) for \(\mathrm{Cs}\)). Inner electronic shells are progressively added, which shield the outermost electron from nuclear attraction and move the valence shell farther from the nucleus.

Step 3: Verification with experimental values
The experimental atomic radii are: \(\mathrm{Li} = 152\text{ pm}\), \(\mathrm{Na} = 186\text{ pm}\), \(\mathrm{K} = 231\text{ pm}\), \(\mathrm{Rb} = 244\text{ pm}\), and \(\mathrm{Cs} = 262\text{ pm}\).

Therefore, the correct sequence of increasing atomic radius is: \(\mathrm{Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q03 - Increasing order of elemental metallic character

questiontext.text:
Considering their atomic numbers and positions in the Periodic Table, arrange the following elements in the correct sequence of increasing metallic character:

\(\mathrm{Si,\ Be,\ Mg,\ Na,\ P}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify periodic positions of the elements
The elements belong to the second and third periods: \(\mathrm{Be}\) (Group 2, Period 2), \(\mathrm{Na}\) (Group 1, Period 3), \(\mathrm{Mg}\) (Group 2, Period 3), \(\mathrm{Si}\) (Group 14, Period 3), and \(\mathrm{P}\) (Group 15, Period 3).

Step 2: Apply periodic laws of metallic character
Metallic character decreases across a period from left to right because increasing effective nuclear charge holds valence electrons more tightly, disfavoring cation formation. Metallic character increases down a group because atomic size increases and ionization enthalpy decreases, making electron loss easier.

Step 3: Sequential evaluation of third-period elements
Across the third period from left to right, metallic character decreases in the order: \(\mathrm{Na > Mg > Si > P}\). Phosphorus is a non-metal, silicon is a metalloid/semi-metal, and magnesium and sodium are metals.

Step 4: Comparison between group 2 members
Comparing \(\mathrm{Be}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) in Group 2, metallic character increases down the group, so \(\mathrm{Mg > Be}\). Beryllium, located in Period 2, is more metallic than the metalloid silicon (\(\mathrm{Be > Si}\)) but less metallic than magnesium.

Therefore, the correct sequence of increasing metallic character is: \(\mathrm{P < Si < Be < Mg < Na}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q04 - Increasing ionic radii of isoelectronic species

questiontext.text:
Consider the following isoelectronic ions each possessing 10 electrons:

\(\mathrm{N^{3-},\ O^{2-},\ F^-,\ Na^+,\ Mg^{2+},\ Al^{3+}}\)

Which option represents the correct sequence of these ions arranged in order of increasing ionic radius?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify electron count and nuclear charges
All six species have the identical electronic configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) (10 electrons). Their atomic numbers (nuclear charges \(Z\)) are: \(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(Z=13\)), \(\mathrm{Mg}\) (\(Z=12\)), \(\mathrm{Na}\) (\(Z=11\)), \(\mathrm{F}\) (\(Z=9\)), \(\mathrm{O}\) (\(Z=8\)), and \(\mathrm{N}\) (\(Z=7\)).

Step 2: Governing electrostatic principle for isoelectronic species
In an isoelectronic series, the number of electrons is constant. As positive nuclear charge (\(Z\)) increases, the electrostatic attraction exerted by the nucleus on the electron cloud increases, pulling electrons inward and decreasing ionic radius. Conversely, greater negative charge means lower nuclear charge relative to electrons, resulting in greater electron repulsion and expanded radius.

Step 3: Quantitative radii comparison
\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) with \(Z=13\) has the smallest radius (53.5 pm), followed by \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) with \(Z=12\) (72 pm), \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) with \(Z=11\) (95 pm), \(\mathrm{F^-}\) with \(Z=9\) (136 pm), \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) with \(Z=8\) (140 pm), and \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) with \(Z=7\) (171 pm).

Therefore, the correct sequence of increasing ionic radius is: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+} < Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-} < N^{3-}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q05 - Sequential order of second period ionization enthalpies

questiontext.text:
The elements of the second period exhibit notable deviations in their first ionization enthalpies (\(\Delta_i H\)).

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of all eight second-period elements arranged in order of increasing first ionization enthalpy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: General periodic trend
Across the second period from lithium to neon, the first ionization enthalpy generally increases due to increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius.

Step 2: Anomaly between Beryllium and Boron
Beryllium (\(1s^2 2s^2\)) has a fully filled \(2s\) subshell. Boron (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\)) has an electron in a \(2p\) subshell which is less penetrating and more shielded by inner \(1s\) and \(2s\) electrons. Consequently, removing a \(2p\) electron from boron requires less energy than removing a \(2s\) electron from beryllium, making \(\mathrm{B < Be}\) (801 vs 899 kJ mol\(^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Anomaly between Nitrogen and Oxygen
Nitrogen (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\)) has an extra-stable half-filled \(2p\) subshell with three unpaired electrons. Oxygen (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\)) contains two paired electrons in one \(2p\) orbital. Electron-electron repulsion between these paired electrons facilitates electron removal, making \(\mathrm{O < N}\) (1314 vs 1402 kJ mol\(^{-1}\)).

Step 4: Assembling the complete sequence
Combining the regular trend with both anomalies yields the experimental values: \(\mathrm{Li}\) (520) < \(\mathrm{B}\) (801) < \(\mathrm{Be}\) (899) < \(\mathrm{C}\) (1086) < \(\mathrm{O}\) (1314) < \(\mathrm{N}\) (1402) < \(\mathrm{F}\) (1681) < \(\mathrm{Ne}\) (2080 kJ mol\(^{-1}\)).

Therefore, the correct sequence of increasing first ionization enthalpy is: \(\mathrm{Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne}\)
\(\mathrm{Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F < Ne}\)
\(\mathrm{Li < B < Be < C < N < O < F < Ne}\)
\(\mathrm{B < Li < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q06 - Increasing order of negative electron gain enthalpies

questiontext.text:
Consider the elements: \(\mathrm{P}\), \(\mathrm{S}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\), and \(\mathrm{F}\).

Which of the following correctly arranges these elements in sequence from least negative to most negative electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{eg}H\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: General periodic behavior of electron gain enthalpy
Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative across a period from left to right due to increasing effective nuclear charge and smaller atomic size, and becomes less negative down a group due to increasing atomic radius.

Step 2: Comparison between Phosphorus and Sulphur
Phosphorus has an electronic configuration of \([Ne] 3s^2 3p^3\) with a stable, half-filled \(3p\) subshell, resulting in a low tendency to gain an electron. Its electron gain enthalpy is least negative (\(-74\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Sulphur (\([Ne] 3s^2 3p^4\)) readily accepts an electron, with \(\Delta_{eg}H = -200\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Comparison between Fluorine and Chlorine
Although fluorine is above chlorine in Group 17, adding an electron to the very small, compact \(2p\) orbital of fluorine causes strong interelectronic repulsion. In chlorine, the added electron enters the more spacious \(3p\) orbital where electron-electron repulsion is much less. Consequently, chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) than fluorine (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 4: Arranging from least negative to most negative
Ordering the values: \(\mathrm{P}\) (\(-74\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) < \(\mathrm{S}\) (\(-200\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) < \(\mathrm{F}\) (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) < \(\mathrm{Cl}\) (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Therefore, the correct sequence from least negative to most negative electron gain enthalpy is: \(\mathrm{P < S < F < Cl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q07 - Relative sequence of elemental nonmetallic character

questiontext.text:
Consider the elements: \(\mathrm{B}\), \(\mathrm{C}\), \(\mathrm{N}\), \(\mathrm{F}\), and \(\mathrm{Si}\).

Which of the following displays these elements arranged in the correct sequence of increasing non-metallic character?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principles governing non-metallic character
Non-metallic character is directly correlated with electronegativity and the tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons. It increases across a period from left to right as effective nuclear charge increases, and decreases down a group as atomic size increases.

Step 2: Comparison across the second period
For the elements in the second period (\(\mathrm{B}\), \(\mathrm{C}\), \(\mathrm{N}\), \(\mathrm{F}\)), non-metallic character increases progressively from left to right: \(\mathrm{B < C < N < F}\). Fluorine is the most electronegative and most non-metallic element with a Pauling value of 4.0.

Step 3: Comparison between Boron and Silicon
Silicon is in the third period (Group 14), located below carbon. While carbon is a typical non-metal, silicon is a semi-metal/metalloid with a Pauling electronegativity of 1.8. Boron, having an electronegativity of 2.0, has a slightly higher non-metallic character than silicon, placing silicon as the least non-metallic among the given set.

Step 4: Assembling the complete sequence
Combining these relationships yields the progressive sequence of increasing non-metallic character: \(\mathrm{Si < B < C < N < F}\).

Therefore, the correct sequence of increasing non-metallic character is: \(\mathrm{Si < B < C < N < F}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATION_OF_ELEMENTS_AND_PERIODICITY_IN_PROPERTIES_MCQ_Q08 - Decreasing sequence of oxidizing ability of nonmetals

questiontext.text: Considering the non-metallic elements \(\mathrm{F}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\), \(\mathrm{O}\), and \(\mathrm{N}\), which option gives the correct sequence of their chemical reactivity in terms of decreasing oxidizing property?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Concept of oxidizing property
The oxidizing ability of a non-metal reflects its power to accept electrons and undergo reduction. It depends directly on electronegativity, electron gain enthalpy, and bond dissociation enthalpy.

Step 2: Position of Fluorine
Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (4.0 on the Pauling scale) and a low \(\mathrm{F-F}\) bond dissociation energy, making it the strongest oxidizing agent among all known chemical elements.

Step 3: Comparison between Oxygen and Chlorine
Oxygen has the second highest electronegativity (3.5), whereas chlorine has an electronegativity of 3.0. In chemical reactions and displacement processes in solution and gas phase, oxygen acts as a more powerful oxidizing agent than chlorine (as seen in oxide formation and electronegativity scales).

Step 4: Position of Nitrogen
Nitrogen has an electronegativity of 3.0 and forms an extraordinarily stable triple bond (\(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\)) with a very high bond dissociation enthalpy (946 kJ mol\(^{-1}\)), rendering it chemically inert at room temperature with the weakest oxidizing property among the four.

Therefore, the correct sequence of decreasing oxidizing property is: \(\mathrm{F > O > Cl > N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q01 - Middle element atomic weight in Dobereiner triads

questiontext.text: In Dobereiner's Law of Triads, the atomic weight of the middle element is approximately equal to the arithmetic mean of the atomic weights of the other two elements. For the triad consisting of lithium (atomic weight \(7\)), sodium, and potassium (atomic weight \(39\)), what is the expected atomic weight of sodium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify given data
The atomic weight of lithium is given as \(7\) and the atomic weight of potassium is given as \(39\).

Step 2: Apply Dobereiner's Law of Triads
According to Dobereiner's Law of Triads, the atomic weight of the central element (sodium) is approximately the arithmetic mean of the first and third elements:
\[ \text{Atomic weight of Na} = \frac{7 + 39}{2} = \frac{46}{2} = 23 \]

Step 3: Verification with experimental value
The experimental atomic weight of sodium is \(23\), which exactly matches the calculated average.

Final Answer: The expected atomic weight of sodium is \(23\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q02 - Limiting element for Newlands law of octaves

questiontext.text: John Newlands proposed the Law of Octaves in 1865, stating that every eighth element exhibits properties similar to the first element when arranged in increasing order of atomic weights. According to the textbook, this law was found to be valid only up to which element?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand Newlands' Law of Octaves
Newlands arranged known elements in increasing order of atomic weight and noted that every eighth element resembles the first, analogous to octaves of music.

Step 2: Identify the limitation of the law
As stated in the textbook, the repeating relationship of octaves holds true only for lighter elements up to calcium (atomic weight \(40\)). Beyond calcium, transition elements intervene and every eighth element no longer possesses similar properties.

Final Answer: Newlands' Law of Octaves was valid only up to calcium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q03 - Fundamental basis of Mendeleev periodic law

questiontext.text: Dmitri Mendeleev published the Periodic Law for the first time in 1869. According to Mendeleev's original Periodic Law, the physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall Mendeleev's Periodic Law
Dmitri Mendeleev formulated his classification by arranging elements in horizontal rows and vertical columns based on recurring similarities in properties.

Step 2: Identify the governing physical quantity
Mendeleev's Periodic Law explicitly states: 'The properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.' Mendeleev used atomic weights as the organizing basis because atomic structure and atomic numbers were unknown at the time.

Final Answer: Properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q04 - Fundamental basis of modern periodic law

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly expresses the Modern Periodic Law as formulated following Henry Moseley's work?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the basis of the Modern Periodic Law
Following Henry Moseley's discovery that atomic number is a more fundamental property of an atom than atomic mass, Mendeleev's Periodic Law was revised.

Step 2: State the Modern Periodic Law
The Modern Periodic Law states: 'The physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.'

Final Answer: The physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

answer.text: The physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic weights.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q05 - Moseley characteristic X ray spectral relationship

questiontext.text: In 1913, Henry Moseley examined the characteristic X-ray spectra of various elements. A straight line was obtained when which of the following mathematical functions of the emitted X-ray frequency (\(\nu\)) was plotted against the atomic number (\(Z\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall Moseley's experimental investigation
Henry Moseley bombarded various target elements with high-energy cathode rays and analyzed the characteristic X-rays emitted.

Step 2: Identify the linear relationship plotted
Moseley discovered that plotting the square root of the frequency of the emitted X-rays, \(\sqrt{\nu}\), against atomic number \(Z\) resulted in a straight line, according to the relation \(\sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)\). A plot against atomic mass did not give a linear relation, proving that atomic number is the fundamental characteristic.

Final Answer: A straight line was obtained for the plot of \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against atomic number \(Z\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q06 - IUPAC nomenclature of element one hundred twenty

questiontext.text: According to the IUPAC systematic nomenclature for elements with atomic number greater than \(100\), what is the official systematic name and three-letter symbol for the element with \(Z = 120\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the numerical roots for each digit
The atomic number is \(120\). The IUPAC numerical root for \(1\) is 'un', for \(2\) is 'bi', and for \(0\) is 'nil'.

Step 2: Assemble the roots and append suffix
Putting the roots together in order gives 'un' + 'bi' + 'nil' + 'ium' = 'unbinilium'.

Step 3: Construct the three-letter symbol
The abbreviation of each root provides the symbol: 'u' for un, 'b' for bi, and 'n' for nil, yielding 'Ubn'.

Final Answer: The IUPAC systematic name is unbinilium and its symbol is Ubn.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q07 - Pauling scale reference electronegativity value

questiontext.text: On the Pauling electronegativity scale, which element was arbitrarily assigned the highest value of \(4.0\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the Pauling electronegativity scale
Electronegativity is a qualitative measure of the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electron pairs to itself.

Step 2: Identify the benchmark standard
Linus Pauling assigned an arbitrary electronegativity value of \(4.0\) to fluorine, which is the most electronegative of all elements.

Final Answer: Fluorine was assigned the value of \(4.0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q08 - Maximum covalency of second period elements

questiontext.text: What is the maximum covalency that can be exhibited by the representative elements of the second period (such as boron or carbon)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the available valence orbitals
Second period elements have principal quantum number \(n = 2\). The only available valence orbitals in the second shell are one \(2s\) orbital and three \(2p\) orbitals.

Step 2: Relate orbital availability to maximum covalency
Since there are only four orbitals in the valence shell (\(1 + 3 = 4\)) and no d-orbitals exist for \(n = 2\), second period elements can accommodate at most four pairs of electrons, limiting their maximum covalency to \(4\).

Final Answer: The maximum covalency of second period elements is \(4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q09 - General outer electronic configuration of d block

questiontext.text: What is the general outer electronic configuration of d-block elements (with the known exception of palladium)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the orbital filling in d-block elements
In d-block elements, electrons enter the penultimate \((n-1)d\) subshell while the outermost shell is \(ns\).

Step 2: State the general configuration
Across Groups 3 to 12, the penultimate d-subshell accommodates 1 to 10 electrons while the outermost s-subshell contains 0 to 2 electrons, giving the general outer configuration \((n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}\).

Final Answer: The general outer electronic configuration is \((n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q10 - Nomenclature of rows and columns in modern table

questiontext.text: In the modern long form of the periodic table, the horizontal rows and vertical columns are designated respectively as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the structure of the modern periodic table
The modern periodic table organizes elements into a two-dimensional grid of horizontal rows and vertical columns.

Step 2: Define periods and groups
The horizontal rows (which Mendeleev originally termed series) are called periods. The vertical columns containing elements with similar outer electronic configurations are called groups or families.

Final Answer: Horizontal rows are periods and vertical columns are groups.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q11 - Lothar Meyer observation on repeating pattern length

questiontext.text: Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties such as atomic volume, melting point, and boiling point against atomic weight and obtained a periodically repeated pattern. What critical observation did Lothar Meyer make regarding this repeating pattern that distinguished his work from Newlands' octaves?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand Lothar Meyer's curve
Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties like atomic volume against atomic weight, producing periodic curves where chemically similar elements occupied corresponding positions.

Step 2: Contrast with Newlands' Law of Octaves
While Newlands assumed a fixed octave interval of eight elements throughout, Lothar Meyer observed that the length of the repeating pattern actually changes as atomic weight increases, which closely anticipated the modern periods of varying lengths.

Final Answer: Lothar Meyer observed a change in the length of the repeating pattern.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q12 - Mendeleev prediction for eka aluminium oxide formula

questiontext.text: Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap below aluminium in his periodic table and named the undiscovered element Eka-aluminium. This element was later discovered and its predicted oxide formula matched the experimental finding. Which element corresponds to Eka-aluminium and what is the formula of its oxide?

generalfeedback.text:

Mendeleev predicted an element directly below aluminium with an atomic weight near \(68\), which he termed Eka-aluminium.

Step 2: Correlate with discovered element and oxide formula
Eka-aluminium was discovered in 1875 as gallium (Ga). Mendeleev predicted its oxide to be \(E_2O_3\), which was verified experimentally by the formula of gallium oxide, \(\mathrm{Ga_2O_3}\).

Final Answer: Gallium with the oxide formula \(\mathrm{Ga_2O_3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q13 - Mendeleev prediction for eka silicon chloride formula

questiontext.text: Mendeleev predicted the properties of the undiscovered element Eka-silicon, including the formula of its chloride. What was the discovered name of this element and the formula of its chloride?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Eka-silicon
Mendeleev left a gap beneath silicon in Group IV and predicted an element termed Eka-silicon with an atomic weight of about \(72\).

Step 2: Match with discovery and chloride stoichiometry
The element was later discovered as germanium (Ge). Mendeleev predicted a chloride formula of \(E\mathrm{Cl_4}\), which was confirmed experimentally as \(\mathrm{GeCl_4}\).

Final Answer: Germanium with chloride formula \(\mathrm{GeCl_4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q14 - Inversion of atomic weight order in Mendeleev table

questiontext.text: In constructing his periodic table, Mendeleev placed elements with similar chemical properties in the same vertical group, occasionally ignoring the strict order of increasing atomic weights. Which of the following pairs represents such an intentional inversion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall anomalies in Mendeleev's periodic table
Mendeleev prioritized grouping elements by chemical properties over strict adherence to increasing atomic weights.

Step 2: Identify the inverted pair from the text
Tellurium has an atomic weight of \(127.6\) while iodine has an atomic weight of \(126.9\). In order to place iodine in Group VII alongside fluorine, chlorine, and bromine, Mendeleev placed tellurium before iodine, inverting the strict order of atomic weights.

Final Answer: Tellurium (atomic weight \(127.6\)) was placed before iodine (atomic weight \(126.9\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q15 - Positioning of helium in periodic table p block

questiontext.text: Although helium has an outermost electronic configuration of \(1s^2\) (which strictly corresponds to the s-block), it is placed in Group 18 of the p-block. What is the justification provided in the textbook for this positioning?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the electronic structure of helium
Helium possesses two electrons occupying the \(1s\) orbital (\(1s^2\)), which completes its first principal energy shell (K shell).

Step 2: Relate electronic configuration to chemical behavior
Because its valence shell is completely filled, helium exhibits characteristic chemical inertness, low reactivity, and gaseous monoatomic nature identical to the noble gases in Group 18 of the p-block.

Final Answer: Helium has a completely filled valence shell and exhibits properties characteristic of noble gases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q16 - Number of orbitals and elements in fifth period

questiontext.text: On the basis of quantum mechanical orbital filling, why does the fifth period of the periodic table contain exactly 18 elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the orbitals available for filling in the fifth period
In the fifth period (\(n = 5\)), the orbitals that are filled in order of increasing energy are \(5s\), \(4d\), and \(5p\).

Step 2: Calculate the total number of available orbitals
The \(5s\) subshell consists of 1 orbital, the \(4d\) subshell consists of 5 orbitals, and the \(5p\) subshell consists of 3 orbitals. The total number of available orbitals is \(1 + 5 + 3 = 9\).

Step 3: Determine the maximum number of electrons
Each orbital can accommodate at most 2 electrons. Therefore, 9 orbitals can accommodate \(9 \times 2 = 18\) electrons, resulting in exactly 18 elements in the fifth period.

Final Answer: Nine orbitals (one \(5s\), five \(4d\), and three \(5p\)) accommodate a maximum of 18 electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q17 - Exceptional electronic configuration of palladium

questiontext.text: While the general outer electronic configuration of d-block elements is \((n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}\), palladium (\(\mathrm{Pd}\), \(Z = 46\)) represents a unique exception. What is the ground-state outer electronic configuration of palladium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the standard expectation for Group 10
Group 10 elements in the 4th and 6th periods (Ni and Pt) typically possess \((n-1)d^8 ns^2\) or \((n-1)d^9 ns^1\) outer configurations.

Step 2: Identify the specific configuration of palladium
In palladium (\(Z = 46\)), both electrons from the \(5s\) subshell shift into the \(4d\) subshell to achieve a completely filled, energetically stable \(4d^{10}\) subshell. Hence, the outer electronic configuration of Pd is \(4d^{10}5s^0\).

Final Answer: The outer electronic configuration of palladium is \(4d^{10}5s^0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q18 - Non transition behavior of zinc cadmium and mercury

questiontext.text: Which group of d-block elements with outer electronic configuration \((n-1)d^{10}ns^2\) does not exhibit typical transition metal properties such as variable oxidation states and paramagnetic behavior?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the characteristics of transition elements
Transition elements are characterized by partially filled d-orbitals in their elemental state or in common oxidation states, which enable variable valence, colored ions, and paramagnetism.

Step 2: Identify the exceptional elements
Zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), and mercury (Hg) belonging to Group 12 have completely filled \((n-1)d^{10}\) subshells in their ground states as well as in their common \(+2\) oxidation states. Consequently, they do not show most typical properties of transition metals.

Final Answer: Zinc, cadmium, and mercury (\(\mathrm{Zn, Cd, Hg}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q19 - Systematic IUPAC name of element one seventeen

questiontext.text: According to the IUPAC systematic nomenclature, what is the temporary name and symbol for the element with atomic number \(117\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the numerical roots for digits 1, 1, and 7
The digit 1 corresponds to 'un', the second digit 1 corresponds to 'un', and the digit 7 corresponds to 'sept'.

Step 2: Combine roots with suffix -ium
Combining the roots gives 'un' + 'un' + 'sept' + 'ium' = 'ununseptium'.

Step 3: Construct the symbol
The first letters of the three roots are 'u', 'u', and 's', giving the symbol 'Uus'.

Final Answer: Ununseptium with symbol Uus.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q20 - Covalent and metallic radii definition and values

questiontext.text: The internuclear distance between two chlorine atoms in a \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) molecule is \(198\text{ pm}\), while the distance between two adjacent copper atoms in solid copper is \(256\text{ pm}\). What are the covalent radius of chlorine and the metallic radius of copper, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Apply the definition of covalent radius
The covalent radius of a non-metal is half the internuclear distance between two atoms bound together by a single covalent bond:
\[ r_{\text{cov}}(\mathrm{Cl}) = \frac{198\text{ pm}}{2} = 99\text{ pm} \]

Step 2: Apply the definition of metallic radius
The metallic radius is half the internuclear distance separating metal cores in a metallic crystal lattice:
\[ r_{\text{met}}(\mathrm{Cu}) = \frac{256\text{ pm}}{2} = 128\text{ pm} \]

Final Answer: The covalent radius of chlorine is \(99\text{ pm}\) and the metallic radius of copper is \(128\text{ pm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q21 - Decrease of atomic radius across second period

questiontext.text: Why does the atomic radius generally decrease across a period from left to right (for example, from lithium to fluorine in the second period)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze electron addition across a period
Across a period, successive electrons are added into orbitals of the same principal quantum shell (\(n = 2\) for the second period).

Step 2: Evaluate effective nuclear charge and shielding
Electrons in the same shell provide poor mutual shielding against the increasing nuclear charge. As atomic number increases, the effective nuclear charge increases progressively, pulling the outer electrons closer to the nucleus and decreasing the atomic radius.

Final Answer: Electrons are added to the same principal shell while effective nuclear charge increases.

answer.text: Principal quantum number increases across the period.
Shielding of core electrons increases more rapidly than nuclear charge.
Electrons are added to the same shell while effective nuclear charge increases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q22 - Order of increasing ionic radii for isoelectronic species

questiontext.text: Consider the isoelectronic species \(\mathrm{N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^-, Na^+, Mg^{2+}}\), and \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\), all having 10 electrons. What is the correct order of these ions arranged in increasing ionic radius?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the electron count and nuclear charges
All six species possess 10 electrons. The nuclear charges (\(Z\)) are: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 13\)), \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 12\)), \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) (\(Z = 11\)), \(\mathrm{F^-}\) (\(Z = 9\)), \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) (\(Z = 8\)), and \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) (\(Z = 7\)).

Step 2: Relate nuclear charge to ionic radius in isoelectronic species
For isoelectronic ions, greater positive nuclear charge exerts a stronger inward attraction on the electron cloud, reducing ionic radius. Conversely, lower nuclear charge with high negative charge expands the ion due to increased electron-electron repulsion.

Step 3: Arrange in increasing order
Therefore, the ionic radius increases with decreasing nuclear charge: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+} < Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-} < N^{3-}}\).

Final Answer: The correct increasing order is \(\mathrm{Al^{3+} < Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-} < N^{3-}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q23 - Ionization enthalpy anomaly between boron and beryllium

questiontext.text: Even though boron (\(Z = 5\)) has a greater nuclear charge than beryllium (\(Z = 4\)), the first ionization enthalpy of boron (\(801\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is lower than that of beryllium (\(899\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). What is the primary reason for this anomaly?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Write the ground-state electronic configurations
Beryllium has the electronic configuration \(1s^2 2s^2\) and boron has \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\).

Step 2: Compare orbital penetration and shielding
The electron removed from beryllium is an s-electron, whereas the electron removed from boron is a p-electron. In the same shell, an s-electron penetrates closer to the nucleus than a p-electron. The \(2p\) electron of boron is effectively shielded by both the inner \(1s\) core and the \(2s\) electrons, making it easier to remove.

Final Answer: The \(2p\) electron in boron is more shielded and penetrates less to the nucleus than the \(2s\) electron in beryllium.

answer.text: Boron has a lower nuclear charge than beryllium.
Beryllium has half-filled p-orbitals which confer extra stability.
The \(2p\) electron of boron penetrates less and is more shielded than the \(2s\) electron of beryllium.
Boron is a metalloid whereas beryllium is an alkaline earth metal.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q24 - Ionization enthalpy anomaly between oxygen and nitrogen

questiontext.text: The first ionization enthalpy of oxygen (\(1314\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is smaller than that of nitrogen (\(1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), contrary to the general periodic trend. What explains this difference?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Compare electronic configurations
Nitrogen (\(Z = 7\)) has the configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\) with three half-filled \(2p\) orbitals. Oxygen (\(Z = 8\)) has \(1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1\).

Step 2: Evaluate electron-electron repulsion
In oxygen, two electrons must share the same \(2p\) orbital, causing increased mutual repulsion between them. This inter-electronic repulsion makes it easier to remove the fourth \(2p\) electron from oxygen compared to removing an electron from the stable, half-filled configuration of nitrogen.

Final Answer: In oxygen, pairing of electrons in a \(2p\) orbital causes increased electron-electron repulsion.

answer.text: Oxygen has smaller nuclear charge than nitrogen.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q25 - Electron gain enthalpy anomaly fluorine versus chlorine

questiontext.text: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of fluorine (\(-328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) less negative than that of chlorine (\(-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the shells receiving the added electron
In fluorine, the incoming electron enters the compact \(n = 2\) energy level (\(2p\) subshell), whereas in chlorine it enters the larger \(n = 3\) level (\(3p\) subshell).

Step 2: Compare inter-electronic repulsion
Due to the small size of the \(2p\) orbitals in fluorine, the electron cloud density is high and the added electron experiences significant electrostatic repulsion from the existing electrons. In chlorine, the larger \(3p\) volume reduces repulsion, allowing chlorine to release more energy upon electron addition.

Final Answer: The compact \(2p\) subshell in fluorine causes significant electron-electron repulsion on the added electron.

answer.text: Fluorine has a lower electronegativity than chlorine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASSIFICATIONOFELEMENTSANDPERIODICITYINPROPERTIES_MCQ_Q26 - Positive electron gain enthalpy of noble gases

questiontext.text: Why do noble gas elements exhibit large positive electron gain enthalpies?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the ground-state electronic configuration of noble gases
Noble gases possess completely filled valence shells (\(ns^2 np^6\), or \(1s^2\) for helium), which represent highly stable closed-shell electronic configurations.

Step 2: Consider the destination of an additional electron
An added electron cannot enter the filled valence shell; it must occupy an orbital in the next higher principal quantum shell (\(n + 1\)). Because this higher orbital experiences strong shielding and is energetically unfavorable, energy must be supplied to force the electron into the atom, resulting in an endothermic process with a positive electron gain enthalpy.

Final Answer: The added electron must enter the next higher principal quantum level leading to an unstable configuration.
